sentences.text: This man looks deep in prayer, but he may not be alive.
This is Saint Francis of Assisi in His Tomb, painted by Francisco de Zurbarán.
Most people see a friar praying over a human skull.
The painting belongs to the Milwaukee Art Museum.
And the picture seems to agree.
His hands hold the skull, and one bare foot steps forward.
His face has almost vanished into shadow.
According to a tradition popular in the seventeenth century, a pope opened Francis's tomb at Assisi.
He found the body miraculously preserved, standing upright in the tomb.
Zurbarán painted that vision for the Count Duke of Olivares.
He isn't a monk at prayer.
He's a dead saint, still standing in his grave.
So is he praying, or has he been standing there for centuries?

meta.title: They Opened His Tomb... and He Was Still STANDING #history #art
meta.description: Saint Francis of Assisi in His Tomb was painted by Francisco de Zurbarán between 1630 and 1634 and hangs in the Milwaukee Art Museum. It follows a tradition that the saint's body was found preserved and standing upright when his tomb was opened.
meta.question: Praying, or standing there for centuries?

sources.claim: Saint Francis of Assisi in His Tomb is an oil-on-canvas painting by the Spanish Baroque artist Francisco de Zurbarán, created between 1630 and 1634.
Description and origins The painting depicts Saint Francis of Assisi standing in a dark space while contemplating a human skull.
The work is part of the permanent collection of the Milwaukee Art Museum and is regarded as one of the most important examples of seventeenth-century Spanish art in an American collection.
Zurbarán employs dramatic chiaroscuro, illuminating the saint’s coarse Franciscan habit, face, skull, and protruding foot against a nearly black background.
According to a tradition popular in the 17th century, as Pope Nicholas V visited Assisi in 1449 and the saint's tomb was opened, he saw the body of Francis miraculously preserved and standing upright
